fields.v: Claudino, B., Xing, R., Zuo, Y., Menezes, T., Sarma, A., Damevski, K., Feng, Z. (2026). The EPIC Framework for Spec-Driven Development. arXiv:2610.07534v1 [cs.SE], 6 Oct 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2610.07534v1 [cs.SE]; ACM template with placeholder header '111:x Trovato et al.', venue not stated
Virginia Commonwealth University (Claudino, Zuo, Damevski, Feng); Oregon State University (Xing, Sarma); CodeDay (Menezes)

Proposes an approach; secondary: Evaluates — EPIC framework of 40 specification-writing practices in 10 quality dimensions and 4 categories, with a 0-3 scoring rubric and an agent skill (review and authoring modes); evaluated by mixed methods: rubric scoring of 114 OSS SDD repositories, grey-literature review of 30 sources, practitioner interviews (N=15), observational association of spec-quality scores with SonarQube/GitHub outcomes
fields.why: Still a judgement. EPIC is offered as practices that 'guide developers' plus an authoring skill (an approach to writing specs), but its 0-3 rubric is also used to score 114 repositories, i.e. a spec-quality evaluation method. If 'Proposes an evaluation method' becomes the main nature, Q13 becomes N/A.

fields.v: EPIC (Expressive, Precise, Interpretable, Compartmentalized) framework for SDD specification quality; version Not stated. Also an EPIC agent skill (SKILL.md + references) with review and authoring modes. Repositories studied use Spec Kit, OpenSpec or no dedicated framework (versions Not stated)

EPIC prescribes no artefacts of its own; it gives quality practices for the SDD artefact set: specification, plan and tasks (also context files such as AGENTS.md in the skill example). Practices include [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers, measurable bounds, normative MUST/SHALL wording, stable unique requirement IDs, explicit template declaration, verification criteria and completion conditions, dependency/failure handling, requirements-to-implementation traceability

Not prescribed (EPIC is a quality framework, not a workflow). Skill: review mode (scores each dimension 0-3 citing passages) and authoring mode (drafting or revising artefacts, marking unresolved decisions for clarification). Frameworks cited for context: Spec Kit Specify -> Plan -> Tasks -> Implement; Kiro requirements, design, tasks; OpenSpec proposals, specs, designs, tasks, archives

EPIC is meant for developers to review a specification before any code exists; clarification markers flag decisions for the human; suggested CI/CD checks when specs or plans change. No explicit gates defined

Specification format / artefact quality only, document-based: existing artefacts of 114 repositories scored with the rubric; no agent run. The agent skill is shown on two examples only (Fig. 3), its reliability not measured

Not stated / not classifiable. Authors' wording: 'a structured natural-language specification drives the agent's implementation'; specification as 'persistent artifact that mediates collaboration between humans and agents'
N/A (no tasks run); repository artefacts of open-source SDD projects (new and existing code not distinguished)

114 repositories (from 850 candidates, 206 screened); outcomes on 109 (GitHub) and 100 (SonarQube, >=1,000 NCLOC). Median repository: 136 PRs, 50 issues, 6 contributors, 771 commits. 5,675 coded segments

Mixed open-source software (examples: network tooling, prompt-flow editor); English artefacts; >=10 GitHub stars; repository languages not reported (SonarQube analyzers named for Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, Go are examples of the bundled analyzers, not a language breakdown)

Interviews: 15 practitioners with SDD experience (7 backend/full-stack developers, 2 data/ML engineers, 1 QA engineer, 1 system architect, 1 project manager, 1 electrical engineer, 2 software researchers); 14 with >=6 years' experience; 11 use specs/structured context often or very often; 12 used AI tools with written specs >=6 months. Repositories: not stated
None measured
Bugs per KLOC (SonarQube); bug-fix commit rate (share of commits starting with fix:, bugfix, hotfix; repos with >=20 commits)
Vulnerabilities per KLOC and cyclomatic complexity per KLOC (SonarQube, Sonar way profile)
None measured
Specification-quality score 0-30 (10 dimensions x 0-3 rubric); practitioner agreement per practice (5-point Likert); development activity: PRs, merged PRs, issues, contributors, commits

Manual: rubric scoring by two researchers (calibration on 13 + 23 repos; exact agreement 80% / 83%; quadratic-weighted kappa 0.82 / 0.78; Krippendorff alpha 0.94 / 0.80), remaining 78 split between them; interviews with Likert ratings + think-aloud, inductive coding and card sorting. Automatic: SonarQube Community Build 26.9 + SonarScanner CLI 8.0.1 on latest commit (12 Sep 2026); GitHub REST API. Stats: Spearman, one-sided Mann-Whitney U, Cliff's delta, Benjamini-Hochberg

N/A: no approach + agent + model configuration run (unit is the repository / practice). Practitioner assessment: every one of the 40 practices endorsed (agree + strongly agree) by a majority, from 8/15 (E2.1 atomic functional statements) to 14/15 (e.g. E1.4, P2.2, P2.3, I2.1, C2.1). Repository associations: see Comparison: result

Observational, no configurations. Top (>=23) vs bottom (<=18) spec-quality tertile bands (n = 36/24/40 SonarQube; 40/26/43 GitHub) plus Spearman correlation over full range; hypotheses H1-H4. Baseline: bottom band. Held constant: nothing controlled (no multivariate controls); same SonarQube profile per language. Acceptance tests: N/A. Repetitions: single snapshot. Human intervention: N/A

H1 bugs/KLOC: rho = -0.183 (p = 0.035), but bands 0.235 vs 0.248 (-5.1%, p = 0.101, n.s.). H2 vulnerabilities/KLOC: 0.092 vs 0.178 (-48.0%, p = 0.016, delta = -0.286); rho = -0.134 (p = 0.092, n.s.). H3 complexity/KLOC: 137.2 vs 162.3 (-15.4%, p = 0.001, delta = -0.419); rho = -0.206 (p = 0.021). H4: bug-fix commit rate 11.8% vs 20.4% (pBH = 0.034; rho = -0.210, pBH = 0.046); contributors 12.5 vs 3; PRs 202.5 vs 89; all activity measures significant (pBH <= 0.048)

Distinguished bands on vulnerabilities, complexity, bug-fix rate and activity; not on bug density between bands. Repeatable: replication package with rubric, data and skill; one snapshot. Limitations stated: small sample, no multivariate controls, confounders (and possible reverse causation), SonarQube varies across languages, correlational only

May have missed dimensions/practices; researcher judgement in scoring and exemplar selection; participants did not apply EPIC in their own projects; associations observational with confounders; public English repos limit generalisability; skill's reliability not measured. Future: evaluate EPIC in real development (incl. student capstones), benchmarks of how agents act on specs that include, weaken or omit practices

Values from Table 1 (p. 15) and text pp. 15-16; Table 1 and Fig. 2 columns jumbled in text extraction, mapped from the text. Abstract '4x as many contributors' = 12.5 vs 3 medians. Paper alternates 'metrics' and 'practices' for the 40 items. Data: companion website / replication package [8] and framework site epicframework.netlify.app [7] (anonymous refs). Pre-registration: Not stated. IRB approved; $50 gift card. Programming languages: mixed

fields.why: r1 kept N/A, but Q4-Q8 are scored for this study, so it is treated as empirical and Q3 applies; missing agent/model information then scores down rather than N/A. Partly matches the reading used for rayyan-800485926 (also observational, tool versions given, practitioners' agents not identified). Author to fix one reading for both.
